blocks.text: Data deduplication is the process of finding and removing repeated or near identical examples from a fine-tuning dataset, examples that add volume without adding genuinely new signal for the model to learn from.

Duplicates are easy to overlook, especially in datasets pulled from production logs, but they can quietly skew a fine-tuned model behavior and, more seriously, leak between training and evaluation splits in ways that make results look better than they actually are.
1. Why Duplicates Quietly Hurt Fine-Tuning

blocks.alt: Duplicate examples get overweighted in training, skewing model behavior

blocks.text: If the same example, or something very close to it, appears many times in a training set, the model effectively sees it more often than other examples during training, giving it disproportionate influence over what the model learns.

This can push a fine-tuned model toward overfitting on whatever pattern the duplicated examples happen to represent, at the expense of the broader range of behavior the rest of the dataset was meant to teach.
2. Exact Duplicates, The Easy Case

blocks.alt: Identical text is flagged as an exact duplicate

blocks.text: Exact duplicates, examples with identical text, are the simplest case to detect and remove, since a straightforward text comparison or hash check reliably catches them without any ambiguity.
Even so, exact duplicates are worth explicitly checking for, since they show up more often than expected, especially when combining data pulled from multiple overlapping sources.
3. Near Duplicates, The Harder Case

blocks.alt: Text that is mostly similar but not identical gets flagged as a near duplicate

blocks.text: Near duplicates, examples that differ only slightly, a rephrased sentence, a changed name, a minor formatting difference, are harder to catch, since a simple exact text match will not flag them, yet they still carry much of the same redundant signal as an exact duplicate.
Catching near duplicates usually requires a similarity based approach rather than exact matching, covered directly in a later section of this topic.
4. Hashing for Exact Duplicate Detection

blocks.alt: Raw text passes through a hash function to produce a hash value

blocks.text: A practical way to find exact duplicates at scale is computing a hash of each example text, then checking for any hash values that appear more than once, an approach that scales easily to millions of examples since comparing hash values is far cheaper than comparing raw text directly.

code.content:
# A simple exact duplicate check using hashing
import hashlib

seen_hashes = set()
deduplicated = []
for example in dataset:
    text_hash = hashlib.sha256(example.text.encode()).hexdigest()
    if text_hash not in seen_hashes:
        seen_hashes.add(text_hash)
        deduplicated.append(example)

blocks.text: 5. Embedding Similarity for Near Duplicate Detection

blocks.alt: An example embedding produces a similarity score, leading to a near duplicate flag

blocks.text: Near duplicates are typically detected by converting each example into an embedding, then measuring how similar those embeddings are to each other, flagging pairs above a chosen similarity threshold as likely near duplicates.
This approach can catch rephrased or lightly edited duplicates that exact text matching would miss entirely, at the cost of more compute than a simple hash comparison.

blocks.text: 6. Duplicates Across Train and Evaluation Splits

blocks.alt: A training example that also appears in the evaluation set is a leakage risk

blocks.text: The most serious deduplication problem is not duplicates within the training set, it is a training example, or a near duplicate of one, ending up in the evaluation set as well. This leaks information and produces evaluation results that look better than the model true generalization ability.

blocks.title: Deduplicate across splits, not just within training
blocks.content: A deduplication pass should always check for overlap between the training set and the evaluation or test sets, not only for duplicates sitting inside the training set alone.

blocks.text: 7. Deduplication Thresholds, How Similar Is Too Similar

blocks.alt: A threshold that is too strict is compared against one that is too loose

blocks.text: Choosing a similarity threshold for near duplicate detection involves a real tradeoff, a threshold set too strict flags genuinely distinct examples as duplicates and removes useful data, while one set too loose lets meaningfully redundant examples slip through undetected.
Reviewing a sample of flagged pairs near the chosen threshold, checking whether they actually look redundant to a human, is a practical way to calibrate this setting for a specific dataset.
8. When Some Repetition Is Actually Fine

Not all repetition is harmful, a dataset can legitimately contain several distinct examples that share a similar structure because that structure genuinely represents common, important cases in the target task.

The goal of deduplication is removing redundant signal that adds no new information, not eliminating every structural similarity, which is why a naive rule like remove anything similar can backfire if applied too aggressively.
9. Deduplication as Part of the Pipeline

Deduplication fits naturally alongside the cleaning stage covered earlier in this module, and like cleaning, it benefits from being run as a repeatable script rather than a manual one time pass, especially as new data gets added to a growing dataset over time.
Worked Example

A team combining three different sources of support ticket data, a helpdesk export, a chat log export, and a manually curated set, runs an exact hash check first and removes eight hundred identical duplicates that existed across the overlapping sources.

They then run an embedding similarity pass and discover a further four hundred near duplicate pairs, mostly the same ticket logged twice with minor formatting differences between the two export systems. After removing these and confirming no overlap remains between their training and evaluation splits, the resulting dataset is meaningfully smaller but produces a fine-tuned model that generalizes noticeably better than one trained on the raw, undeduplicated combination.
Common Mistakes

items: Checking only for exact duplicates and missing near duplicates that carry similar redundant signal
Never checking for overlap between the training set and the evaluation or test sets
Setting a similarity threshold without reviewing a sample of flagged pairs to calibrate it
Removing every structurally similar example indiscriminately, even when that structure represents genuinely important, distinct cases

blocks.text: Practice

Take a dataset you have access to, even a small one, and manually scan for a handful of near duplicate examples, ones that differ only slightly in wording, and consider whether an exact hash check alone would have caught them.
Key Takeaway

Deduplication removes redundant examples that would otherwise skew training and, more critically, checks for overlap between training and evaluation data that could quietly inflate how good a fine-tuned model appears, and doing this well requires catching both exact duplicates through hashing and near duplicates through similarity comparison.
